name: Daria Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so public remarks and private thoughts can be different. Could you describe an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Daria, forty-three, and I lead an electrical crew wiring homes and repairing shops. I have a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I usually get the difficult fault or the final check nobody wants rushed. I enjoy finding the loose connection that explains three odd symptoms; what wears me out is being halfway home when another coordination call arrives.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things outside the crew?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Alex works in a pottery workshop, and we have children aged eight and twelve and a mortgage. My pay is typical for this trade, we've saved four months of expenses and there are some other electrical firms nearby. I use AI now and then for a draft handover after a colleague has tested the tool, checking it against the actual readings. One afternoon a week I do paid planning and checking records, with the rest mostly on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep the small tool if it earns its place, but don't ask it to become a whole new trade. I'd still want a paid day that includes the checks and the handover. An accurate account of what we tested matters more than a quick page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work and our household money feel secure in this picture. Both wages cover the mortgage and essentials, and four months saved lets us deal with an ordinary setback. I can ask a question about a new process without thinking that every question threatens my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the repair crew now and through the first year, with the same test checks and occasional checked AI handovers. I'd keep the normal family budget and the paid planning afternoon. I wouldn't pay for a new course simply because the news had become less dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and glad to have an ordinary week. Being good at a repair doesn't have to come with a prediction about everybody else's future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does four months saved cover in your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An ordinary home repair or a short interruption in pay, if we watch the spending. It isn't four months free of mortgage payments, food or the children needing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a small tool worth keeping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A finished handover that is accurate and takes less time after all the checking. An AI handover that takes all the saved typing time to correct hasn't saved me much.

say: I'd keep **useful small tools** without expecting them to become a new trade.
I'd keep **checks and handovers** inside the paid day rather than judge only the speed of a page.
think: My **work and money** feel secure with two wages covering the mortgage and essentials.
Our **four-month reserve** covers ordinary setbacks, without removing normal family costs during a wage gap.
do: Keep **crew repairs**, the paid planning afternoon and the same test checks through the first year.
Continue **occasional checked handovers** and the normal household budget without purchasing an unnecessary course.
feel: **Calm**, able to enjoy familiar work without predicting the whole labour market.
S0.quote: An AI handover that takes all the saved typing time to correct hasn't saved me much.
fieldNote: Her **senior competence** and master licence support difficult faults and final checks, while typical pay and moderate savings remain distinct from wealth.
Routine **AI handover checks** continue as existing work, not a new learning commitment or a claim to specialist software authority.

steps.text: Keep leading repairs, paid planning and occasional handovers checked against actual test results

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say planning and records can get quicker without the responsibility for a crew evaporating. I'd ask the owner to separate fewer typing minutes from the decisions and checks still needed. I'd suggest the three crew leads bring actual examples together rather than each argue from memory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid planning afternoon could be cut even if the owner still expects me to coordinate the same jobs on the phone. Most of my work remains physical, but losing that paid block would reduce my own wage. Four months saved gives us response time, not a reason to agree to invisible work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd meet the other two leads and ask them to join a written request for paid coordination time tied to real duties. We'd record a fortnight of planning calls and final checks without sharing customer details outside the firm. In the first year I'd keep repair work and take the joint request to the owner before accepting a reduced paid block, with any changed weekly hours and pay written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and fairly determined to get a plain answer. I don't want to defend slow typing; I want to defend the work somebody still has to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the other leads to agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One record method and one request about paid time, not a promise that everybody must reject every tool. If someone didn't want to join, I wouldn't put that person's name on the letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use an AI system to gather the call records?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use a simple sheet with the time and task, not feed private calls into another system. I don't need a clever tool to count a call that happened after the paid day ended.

say: I'd separate **typing time** from the responsibility and final checks that remain with a crew lead.
I'd ask the **three leads** to bring actual examples together rather than argue separately from memory.
think: My **planning pay could fall** if the paid afternoon disappears while the coordination calls continue.
Our **four-month reserve** buys time to respond, not permission to accept necessary work becoming unpaid.
do: Invite the **other two leads** to a joint written request for paid coordination, using only names of willing participants.
Record **two weeks of calls** and final checks, keeping customer details inside the firm.
Keep **repairs** and take the joint request to the owner before accepting reduced hours, requiring written weekly pay and hours.
feel: **Anxious and determined**, wanting a clear paid-time decision rather than defending slow typing.
S1.quote: I don't need a clever tool to count a call that happened after the paid day ended.
fieldNote: Her **joint request** uses consenting crew leads and coordination records, rather than individual teaching or a general objection to software.
Her **personal income risk** concerns a paid planning block, keeping the physical task mix distinct from office time at risk.

steps.text: Ask willing crew leads to sign a joint paid-coordination request using internal task records
Keep repairs; accept changed hours only after reviewing written weekly pay and hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking work changes in 2028 and physical robots follow around 2031, so both dates belong in our household plan. I'd ask what paid duties the firm actually expects a lead to do. I'd tell the children we are checking choices, not that learning has become pointless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My income could shrink first through planning time and later through physical robot competition. Alex's pottery work is physical too, so I can't assume the other wage stays untouched forever. Four months saved gives us some control, but I still need income at forty-eight when the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now Alex and I would write a budget with twenty percent less from each wage, using our actual bills rather than a guessed mortgage number. We'd pause the uncommitted family car upgrade and keep the current roadworthy car. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep paid repairs and use free household advice if actual earnings no longer cover essentials, checking eligibility and terms before counting any help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but able to work through the figures. Testing a smaller wage on paper isn't the same as deciding we've already lost it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why use twenty percent in the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a first stress test, not a prediction of what either employer will do. We'd also check a larger loss and ask for advice if the actual pay moved; I wouldn't present one neat percentage as the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the reserve to keep the car upgrade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the existing car is safe and works. Keeping the reserve for essentials matters more than pretending a postponed purchase is a family disaster.

say: I'd put **2028 thinking work** and robots around 2031 in the same household conversation without merging their dates.
I'd ask for **actual paid lead duties**, while telling the children we are checking choices rather than giving up.
think: My **income could shrink** through paid planning changes and later physical robot competition.
Alex's **physical pottery work** is not permanent shelter, and four months saved cannot replace ongoing earnings at forty-eight.
do: Test a **twenty-percent wage reduction** with Alex using real bills, treating it as a stress test rather than a forecast.
Pause the **uncommitted car upgrade**, keeping the safe working car and reserve for essentials.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2028 and seek free advice if actual earnings miss essentials, counting help only after checking terms.
feel: **Anxious but engaged**, able to test a budget without treating a possible loss as already certain.
S2.quote: Testing a smaller wage on paper isn't the same as deciding we've already lost it.
fieldNote: The **twenty-percent test** is explicitly a household exercise, not an unsupported quantitative prediction about employment or an employer's actual decision.
The **advice trigger** uses real earnings and essential costs; no benefit, lender concession or untouched second wage is assumed.

steps.text: Pause the uncommitted car upgrade, retaining the safe existing car and reserve for essentials
Use free advice if actual earnings miss essentials, checking eligibility and terms before counting help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives the crew time to agree which paid responsibilities change rather than wait for a new rota to appear. I'd keep the joint request focused on actual work and a written weekly wage. A title isn't a paid task list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid hours could still shrink, but five years gives us more time to check the duties before thinking AI arrives in 2031. Robots follow around 2034, when I'll be fifty-one. I don't want to spend those years buying certificates that nobody has connected to a real paid responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the two other leads to continue the joint paid-coordination request now, with names used only by consent. I'd ask for a six-month review of actual duties and written weekly pay and hours while keeping the repair job. In the first year after 2031 I'd review actual wages and essential bills monthly with Alex, and save sixty extra monthly from future earnings only after essentials are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with more room to check the next decision. I can use five years to ask better questions without pretending the questions are a new wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a short course worth considering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A named practical task the firm actually needs, an instructor, employer-paid fees and my full weekly wage protected. I'm asking for those terms, not enrolling in a course that nobody has offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would sixty go into savings regardless?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd stop the extra transfer if essential costs or lower earnings used that money. I wouldn't borrow or move existing emergency cash to make a new-saving target look successful.

say: I'd ask crew leads to agree **paid responsibilities** before a changed rota arrives.
I'd keep the joint request tied to **actual duties** and written weekly pay rather than a reassuring title.
think: My **hours could shrink**, but five years gives us longer to check paid duties before 2031.
I do not want **unconnected certificates** when robots around 2034 leave me still needing earnings at fifty-one.
do: Continue the **joint paid-time request** with willing leads, using names only with consent.
Keep **repairs** and seek six-month reviews of actual duties with written weekly pay and hours.
Review household income monthly after 2031 and save **60 extra monthly** from future earnings only after essentials.
feel: **Anxious but deliberate**, using the warning for clearer terms rather than counting enquiries as income.
S3.quote: I can use five years to ask better questions without pretending the questions are a new wage.
fieldNote: Her **training question** specifies paid fees and protected wages without treating an unoffered place as an agreed commitment.
The **new saving** uses future surplus only, stopping if necessary bills or lower income absorb it and never relabelling old reserve money.

steps.text: Continue the joint paid-time request with willing leads and consent for names
Keep repairs and seek six-month duty reviews with written weekly pay and hours
Save 60 extra monthly from future earnings only after essentials, stopping if the surplus disappears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the children can explore different kinds of work without being told to copy a job their mother already knows. I'd help them read real offers for paid learning when the time comes. I'd keep asking my own employer what duties and hours it is paying for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own work and our money look secure over the next few years with the major change that far away. I'll be fifty-three when thinking AI arrives in 2036 and fifty-six when robots follow around 2039. The children will be eighteen and twenty-two in 2036, but their possible earnings and our remaining mortgage aren't numbers I can assume now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep repair work now and the six-month paid-duty review request. We'd save sixty extra monthly only from future earnings after essentials, stopping if the real budget no longer allows it. In the first year after 2036 I'd review actual wages and essential bills monthly with Alex before committing to a changed household plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later years, but secure enough with the next few to enjoy this weekend. A longer warning lets the children ask their own questions instead of answer mine for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you automatically seek a different job after 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd compare any actual offer with its written wage, hours, tasks and travel costs before choosing. Looking at an offer doesn't mean I've decided to apply or leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would bring the household review forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fall in either wage or a new essential cost that starts using the reserve. We'd use the real figures immediately rather than wait for a date from the scenario.

say: I'd help the children read **real paid-learning offers** rather than ask them to copy my trade.
I'd keep asking the employer for **paid duties and hours** it can actually specify.
think: My **near-term work and money** look secure with the major thinking change a decade away.
I cannot assume **future child earnings** or a cleared mortgage when robots arrive around 2039 and I'm fifty-six.
do: Keep **repairs** and the six-month request to review actual paid duties and written weekly terms.
Save **60 extra monthly** only from future earnings after essentials, stopping if the budget no longer allows it.
Review **household wages and bills** monthly after 2036 with Alex, sooner if either wage or essential costs change.
feel: **Uneasy about later work**, while near-term security leaves room for the children's own questions and family time.
S4.quote: Looking at an offer doesn't mean I've decided to apply or leave.
fieldNote: Her **offer comparison** is not a chosen job search or departure, and no adult child's possible wage is counted as household income.
The **longer horizon** improves near-term confidence while preserving real review triggers, existing debt uncertainty and the need for earnings beyond age fifty-six.

steps.text: Keep repairs and seek six-month duty reviews with written weekly pay and hours
Save 60 extra monthly from future earnings only after essentials, stopping if the surplus disappears

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because paid planning could change quickly and robots around 2031 could later affect the physical work too. Written duties, weekly pay and hours would help, along with paid practical instruction for an actual new responsibility. I want the wage agreement to be as clear as the test sheet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask where the paid work goes when one visible task becomes quicker. The call still arrives in my car even if the afternoon for answering it has vanished from the rota. A smaller paid block doesn't make the responsibility smaller.

headlineQuote: A smaller paid block doesn't make the responsibility smaller.
portrait: Daria is a **43-year-old crew leader** with a two-year technical diploma and master electrician's licence, handling difficult faults and final checks.
She has **four months saved**, typical pay, some local firms, a mortgage and two schoolchildren with pottery-working partner Alex.
She uses **AI occasionally** after colleague testing, keeping routine checked handovers distinct from a new learning commitment.
Her **joint paid-duty request** responds to possible planning-pay cuts, while longer warnings allow conditional new saving without imagined courses or departures.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could quickly change paid planning, before physical robots around 2031 affect the hands-on work.
whatWouldHelp: Written duties, **weekly pay and hours** plus paid practical instruction for a real new responsibility would help.
